Divine Attributes
dih-VINE AT-rih-byoots
n. phrase (theology proper)
From Latin divinus (of God) + attributum (what is ascribed to a subject); the classical theological term for the perfections — infinite, non-acquired, and essential — that belong to God by virtue of His nature.

Biblical Definition

The divine attributes are the perfections of God revealed in Scripture — what He is, eternally and fully, from Himself and by Himself. Scripture does not offer an abstract philosophical treatise, but its cumulative testimony presents a portrait of infinite perfection: “Before the mountains were born, or You gave birth to the earth and the world — even from everlasting to everlasting, You are God” (Ps 90:2). Reformed theology organizes the divine attributes into two categories: incommunicable (belonging to God alone — aseity, simplicity, immutability, impassibility, eternity, infinity) and communicable (shared by analogy with creatures — wisdom, goodness, love, holiness, justice, truth). The distinction is pedagogically useful but must be held carefully: all of God's attributes are His essence, not parts of Him. Divine simplicity teaches that God is not composed of parts; His love, holiness, omniscience, and justice are all His one simple being, not separate capacities. When Isaiah hears the seraphim cry “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isa 6:3), the threefold repetition signals that holiness is not one attribute alongside others but the key in which all God's perfections are heard. Revelation 4:8 echoes this at the throne-room of eternity. The 1689 London Baptist Confession (2.1) catalogs the classical divine perfections with precision: “most holy, most free, most absolute, infinite in being and perfection, most loving, most gracious.” These are not human projections onto the divine; they are the revealed character of the living God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The perfections that belong to God by virtue of His eternal, infinite nature — including aseity, immutability, omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, holiness, justice, truth, and love — constituting His one simple, undivided essence as the Triune God.

DIVINE ATTRIBUTES, n. phrase. The properties belonging to God by His nature — not acquired, not granted, not capable of increase or diminishment — the perfections of infinite divine being.

Reformed theology divides them into incommunicable (aseity, simplicity, immutability, impassibility, eternity, infinity — belonging to God alone) and communicable (wisdom, goodness, holiness, love, justice, truth — shared by analogy with image-bearers). The division is pedagogical; in God's actual being, the attributes are not parts but one simple essence.

The chief danger in discussing the divine attributes is the projection of human limitation onto God. God's knowledge is not human knowledge with more information added; it is infinite and exhaustive from eternity. His love is not emotional sentiment subject to disappointment; it is eternal, sovereign, and purposive. His justice is not a counterweight to His love; both are expressions of the same holy simplicity.

Scripture names many attributes directly: “God is love” (1 John 4:8); “God is light” (1 John 1:5); the LORD “merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth” (Ex 34:6). Each is a window into the same infinite being.

The 1689 LBCF (2.1): “There is but one only living and true God, who is infinite in being and perfection, a most pure Spirit, invisible, without body, parts, or passions; immutable, immense, eternal, incomprehensible, almighty, most wise, most holy, most free, most absolute; working all things according to the counsel of His own immutable and most righteous will.”

Key Scripture

Psalm 90:2 — "Before the mountains were born, or You gave birth to the earth and the world — even from everlasting to everlasting, You are God."

Exodus 3:14 — "And God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” And He said, “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel, 'I AM has sent me to you.'”"

Isaiah 6:3 — "And one cried to another and said: “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of His glory!”"

Revelation 4:8 — "And the four living creatures, each having six wings, were full of eyes around and within. And they have no rest, day or night, saying: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God Almighty — who was, and who is, and who is to come!”"

Modern Corruption

Open Theism denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge; process theology denies omnipotence and immutability — both domesticate God by making Him dependent on or limited by creation, in direct contradiction of Scripture's self-revealing Lord.

expand to see more

Open Theism (Clark Pinnock, Greg Boyd, John Sanders) denies exhaustive divine foreknowledge: God, they teach, knows all possibilities but not future free choices, and learns from history as it unfolds. This directly contradicts divine aseity, omniscience, and immutability as classically defined. The God who “declares the end from the beginning” (Isa 46:10) does not update His knowledge; the God who “is not a man, that He should lie, nor a son of man, that He should repent” (Num 23:19) does not change His character. Open Theism is not a humble correction of metaphysical overreach; it is a systematic denial of the God who actually revealed Himself in Scripture.

Process theology (A.N. Whitehead, Charles Hartshorne) goes further, denying omnipotence and immutability: God grows, suffers with creation, and is limited by the decisions of His creatures. This is not a more relatable God; it is a different God — one who cannot save, cannot guarantee His promises, and cannot be trusted with the weight of eternity. The Reformed confession of the divine attributes is not Greek philosophy imported into Christianity; it is faithful exegesis of the God who says “I, the LORD, do not change” (Mal 3:6) and whose Son is “the same yesterday and today and forever” (Heb 13:8).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Latin attributum (what is predicated as belonging to a subject's nature); in classical theology, the terms incommunicabilis and communicabilis organize the divine perfections inherited from Scripture.

expand to see more

Latin attributum — what is predicated of a subject as belonging to its nature; used in scholastic theology for the properties necessarily belonging to God.

Latin incommunicabilis — not capable of being shared with creatures; aseity, simplicity, immutability, and impassibility are in this class.

Latin communicabilis — shareable by analogy; wisdom, goodness, love, and justice are communicable because creatures bear a creaturely image of these perfections.

Greek hagiotês — holiness; the seraphic cry of Isa 6:3 and Rev 4:8 makes holiness the central perfection, the key in which all others are heard.

Hebrew 'olam, netsach — everlastingness, eternity; Ps 90:2 uses me'olam ad 'olam (from everlasting to everlasting) to express God's unrestricted, uncaused existence in both temporal directions.

Usage

"The divine attributes are not data for academic systematicians; they are the revealed character of the God with whom every person will one day stand. His holiness demands a perfect substitute; His love provided One."

"Rightly held, the divine attributes destroy both presumption (God's justice will not overlook sin) and despair (God's omnipotence cannot be frustrated; His promises cannot fail)."

"When a congregation loses confidence in the classical divine attributes — trading immutability for emotional responsiveness, omniscience for ‘a God who takes risks’ — they lose the ground under every promise in the Psalms."
